# FDG9027

> DO NOT use `ref` or `out` parameter modifiers in an Async method.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.2.2 Task-Based Async Pattern.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9027
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: verified

Message: Remove the {1} modifier from the parameter '{0}' of the asynchronous method '{2}'

FDG9027 reports a ref or out parameter of an externally visible method that returns a task-like type (as for FDG9020) or IAsyncEnumerable&lt;T>; the compiler already rejects them on async methods (CS1988). Overrides and interface implementations take their signature from another member and are not reported, and private and internal methods are not checked, so coverage is partial. Removing the modifier changes the public signature, so the fix is breaking (FDG9034 describes the conversions); there is no code fix.

## From the book

The .NET runtime only permits value references on the stack (method parameters or locals), which cannot be maintained if an asynchronous method needs to yield execution. The C# compiler understands this limitation, so declaring a `ref` or `out` parameter on a method that uses the `async` keyword is a compile error, but it will not issue an error on arbitrary methods that return Tasks.

```csharp
public Task<bool> TryParseAsync(
  TextReader reader,
  out ParsedData value) {

  Task<ParsedData> parseTask = ParseAsync(reader);

  // This method isn't actually asynchronous;
  // it does a synchronous wait!
  parseTask.Wait();

  if (parseTask.IsFaulted) {
    value = default;
    return Task.FromResult(false);
 }

 value = parseTask.Result;
 return Task.FromResult(true);
}
```

To maintain the ability to write to the `out` parameter, the `TryParseAsync` method instead became a blocking synchronous method masquerading as an asynchronous method. This is not only misleading to the callers of this method, but also can cause deadlock due to the use of `Task.Wait()` (see section 9.2.5.3 for more information).
